nodes.label: Fallacy Lab
nodes.full_label: Fallacy Lab
nodes.summary: Logical fallacies are flaws in reasoning that make an argument weaker than it first appears. They matter because they can make a poor claim sound persuasive, especially in essays, debates, advertising, political speech, social media posts and everyday disagreements.

nodes.label: Ad Hominem
nodes.full_label: When Personal Attacks Replace Reasons | Logical Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: When Personal Attacks Replace Reasons
nodes.summary: Ad hominem arguments shift attention from the claim to the person, often making disagreement less rational.

nodes.label: Association
nodes.full_label: When association replaces evidence | Logical Fallacies 998914 Ad Hominem
nodes.catchy_title: When association replaces evidence
nodes.summary: Associations can mislead when a disliked group or person is used to dismiss a claim without testing its reasons.

nodes.label: Credibility
nodes.full_label: When character evidence actually matters | Logical Fallacies 998914 Ad Hominem
nodes.catchy_title: When character evidence actually matters
nodes.summary: Personal evidence matters only when it bears directly on reliability, expertise, testimony or conflicts of interest.

nodes.label: Pile ons
nodes.full_label: Why online insults spread so fast | Logical Fallacies 998914 Ad Hominem
nodes.catchy_title: Why online insults spread so fast
nodes.summary: Online formats can make a short insult travel faster than a careful rebuttal, changing how audiences judge a claim.

nodes.label: Science Effects
nodes.full_label: Can attacking a scientist change beliefs? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Ad Hominem
nodes.catchy_title: Can attacking a scientist change beliefs?
nodes.summary: Research on attacks against scientists shows personal criticism can reduce confidence in claims even when evidence is untouched.

nodes.label: Tu Quoque Hypocrisy
nodes.full_label: Tu Quoque Hypocrisy | Logical Fallacies 998914 Ad Hominem
nodes.summary: Tu quoque, often translated as “you too”, is a form of ad hominem argument that tries to dismiss a claim, criticism or recommendation by pointing out...

nodes.label: Advertising
nodes.full_label: How Ads Make Weak Claims Persuasive | Logical Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: How Ads Make Weak Claims Persuasive
nodes.summary: Advertising often uses fallacy-like shortcuts that make products feel better supported than the evidence allows.

nodes.label: Bandwagon Ads
nodes.full_label: When Popular Ads Pretend Popular Means Proven | Logical Fallacies 998914 Advertising Fallacie
nodes.catchy_title: When Popular Ads Pretend Popular Means Proven
nodes.summary: Popularity can signal real uptake, but it cannot prove quality, safety or value unless the advert supplies stronger evidence.

nodes.label: Celebrity Ads
nodes.full_label: Why Fame Is Not Product Evidence | Logical Fallacies 998914 Advertising Fallacie
nodes.catchy_title: Why Fame Is Not Product Evidence
nodes.summary: A famous face can make a claim feel credible even when the celebrity has no relevant expertise or representative experience.

nodes.label: Clinical Claims
nodes.full_label: What Does Clinically Proven Actually Prove? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Advertising Fallacie
nodes.catchy_title: What Does Clinically Proven Actually Prove?
nodes.summary: Scientific-sounding advertising claims need details about the test, comparison, sample and result before they can support a conclusion.

nodes.label: Hidden Payments
nodes.full_label: When Sponsored Praise Needs Clear Disclosure | Logical Fallacies 998914 Advertising Fallacie
nodes.catchy_title: When Sponsored Praise Needs Clear Disclosure
nodes.summary: Disclosure rules matter because payment, gifts or brand ties can change how audiences judge an endorsement.

nodes.label: Review Ratings
nodes.full_label: Can Star Ratings Become Manufactured Proof? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Advertising Fallacie
nodes.catchy_title: Can Star Ratings Become Manufactured Proof?
nodes.summary: Star ratings become weak evidence when fake reviews, small samples or filtered feedback make consumer opinion look stronger than it is.

nodes.label: Anecdotes
nodes.full_label: When Is a Story Not Enough? | Logical Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: When Is a Story Not Enough?
nodes.summary: Personal stories can be meaningful but become weak support when used as broad proof without other evidence.

nodes.label: After Treatment
nodes.full_label: Did the Remedy Cause the Recovery? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Anecdotal Evidence
nodes.catchy_title: Did the Remedy Cause the Recovery?
nodes.summary: Feeling better after a remedy does not prove the remedy caused the recovery.

nodes.label: Fair Use
nodes.full_label: How to Use Stories Without Cherry Picking | Logical Fallacies 998914 Anecdotal Evidence
nodes.catchy_title: How to Use Stories Without Cherry Picking
nodes.summary: Stories strengthen an argument when they illustrate supported patterns instead of replacing missing evidence.

nodes.label: False Rule
nodes.full_label: When One Story Starts Sounding Like Proof | Logical Fallacies 998914 Anecdotal Evidence
nodes.catchy_title: When One Story Starts Sounding Like Proof
nodes.summary: Anecdotes mislead when one vivid case is treated as proof of what normally happens.

nodes.label: Medical Signals
nodes.full_label: Can a Patient Story Warn US Early? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Anecdotal Evidence
nodes.catchy_title: Can a Patient Story Warn US Early?
nodes.summary: Patient reports and case stories can reveal possible harms, but they need follow-up evidence before becoming proof.

nodes.label: Vivid Stories
nodes.full_label: Why Vivid Examples Feel So Convincing | Logical Fallacies 998914 Anecdotal Evidence
nodes.catchy_title: Why Vivid Examples Feel So Convincing
nodes.summary: Memorable examples can feel common because they are easy to recall, not because they are statistically typical.

nodes.label: Argument Map
nodes.full_label: Can You Map the Reasoning? | Logical Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: Can You Map the Reasoning?
nodes.summary: Argument mapping helps separate claims, reasons and assumptions so weak links become easier to see.

nodes.label: Citation Gaps
nodes.full_label: When a Scientific Source Does Not Prove the Claim | Logical Fallacies 998914 Argument Mapping
nodes.catchy_title: When a Scientific Source Does Not Prove the Claim
nodes.summary: A source may be real while the conclusion drawn from it goes far beyond what the evidence supports.

nodes.label: Hidden Assumptions
nodes.full_label: What Assumptions Make This Policy Argument Work? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Argument Mapping
nodes.catchy_title: What Assumptions Make This Policy Argument Work?
nodes.summary: Policy arguments often rely on unstated assumptions about incentives, costs, feasibility, and outcomes.

nodes.label: Linked Premises
nodes.full_label: Are These Reasons Independent or One Linked Argument? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Argument Mapping
nodes.catchy_title: Are These Reasons Independent or One Linked Argument?
nodes.summary: Many apparent reasons fail because they only work together, not as separate support for a conclusion.

nodes.label: Policy Objections
nodes.full_label: Do the Objections Undermine the Policy or the Reasoning? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Argument Mapping
nodes.catchy_title: Do the Objections Undermine the Policy or the Reasoning?
nodes.summary: Transport proposals reveal how objections can target evidence, assumptions, trade-offs, or implementation details.

nodes.label: Weak Link Checks
nodes.full_label: Which Part of the Argument Actually Fails? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Argument Mapping
nodes.catchy_title: Which Part of the Argument Actually Fails?
nodes.summary: Systematic checks can reveal whether a problem lies in a premise, inference, assumption, or objection.

nodes.label: Authority
nodes.full_label: When Should You Trust an Expert? | Logical Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: When Should You Trust an Expert?
nodes.summary: Expert opinion can help, but it becomes weak support when expertise is irrelevant, overstated or treated as final.

nodes.label: Biased Experts
nodes.full_label: When Experts Have Something to Gain | Logical Fallacies 998914 Appeal To Authority
nodes.catchy_title: When Experts Have Something to Gain
nodes.summary: Expert opinion becomes less reliable when funding, ideology, or personal incentives are hidden behind professional credentials.

nodes.label: Celebrity Claims
nodes.full_label: When Fame Pretends to Be Expertise | Logical Fallacies 998914 Appeal To Authority
nodes.catchy_title: When Fame Pretends to Be Expertise
nodes.summary: Famous endorsements can feel persuasive, but they often collapse when the celebrity has no relevant expertise for the claim.

nodes.label: Evidence Not Proof
nodes.full_label: Why Experts Still Need Evidence | Logical Fallacies 998914 Appeal To Authority
nodes.catchy_title: Why Experts Still Need Evidence
nodes.summary: Expert testimony can support an argument, but it should guide readers toward evidence rather than replace evidence altogether.

nodes.label: Expert Consensus
nodes.full_label: One Expert or the Whole Field? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Appeal To Authority
nodes.catchy_title: One Expert or the Whole Field?
nodes.summary: One qualified expert may offer useful evidence, but consensus usually carries more weight than an isolated authoritative voice.

nodes.label: Unnamed Experts
nodes.full_label: Who Are These Experts, Exactly? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Appeal To Authority
nodes.catchy_title: Who Are These Experts, Exactly?
nodes.summary: Claims attributed only to unnamed experts are hard to check, making the appeal weaker even when the conclusion might be true.

nodes.label: Bad Samples
nodes.full_label: How Much Evidence Is Enough? | Logical Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: How Much Evidence Is Enough?
nodes.summary: Hasty generalisations draw big conclusions from too little evidence or from examples that are not representative.

nodes.label: Digest Poll
nodes.full_label: The Huge Poll That Got It Wrong | Logical Fallacies 998914 Hasty Generalisation
nodes.catchy_title: The Huge Poll That Got It Wrong
nodes.summary: The 1936 Literary Digest poll shows why a huge number of responses can still mislead when the sample is badly selected.

nodes.label: Experience
nodes.full_label: What Personal Experience Can Prove | Logical Fallacies 998914 Hasty Generalisation
nodes.catchy_title: What Personal Experience Can Prove
nodes.summary: Personal stories can identify real harms and useful leads, but they do not automatically measure how common a problem is.

nodes.label: Review Bias
nodes.full_label: Do Bad Reviews Show the Whole Picture? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Hasty Generalisation
nodes.catchy_title: Do Bad Reviews Show the Whole Picture?
nodes.summary: Online complaints can reveal real problems, but they can also over-represent people motivated enough to post.

nodes.label: Small Samples
nodes.full_label: How Many Examples Are Enough? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Hasty Generalisation
nodes.catchy_title: How Many Examples Are Enough?
nodes.summary: A few real examples can raise a useful question, but they rarely prove a broad claim about a whole group or trend.

nodes.label: Some to Most
nodes.full_label: When Some Becomes Most | Logical Fallacies 998914 Hasty Generalisation
nodes.catchy_title: When Some Becomes Most
nodes.summary: Hasty generalisations often smuggle a claim from 'some' to 'most' when vivid examples fit what people already expect.

nodes.label: Bandwagon
nodes.full_label: Are You Being Pressured to Join? | Logical Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: Are You Being Pressured to Join?
nodes.summary: Bandwagon arguments pressure people to agree by suggesting that everyone else is already on board.

nodes.label: Asch Lines
nodes.full_label: What the Asch Experiments Still Show | Logical Fallacies 998914 Bandwagon Pressure
nodes.catchy_title: What the Asch Experiments Still Show
nodes.summary: The Asch line experiments show how even obvious evidence can feel harder to trust when a unanimous group says otherwise.

nodes.label: Group Knows
nodes.full_label: When Should You Trust the Crowd? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Bandwagon Pressure
nodes.catchy_title: When Should You Trust the Crowd?
nodes.summary: Following the crowd can be reasonable when others have real expertise, but risky when people are only copying one another.

nodes.label: Reach vs Truth
nodes.full_label: When Popularity Is Not Proof | Logical Fallacies 998914 Bandwagon Pressure
nodes.catchy_title: When Popularity Is Not Proof
nodes.summary: A claim can be widely shared, downloaded, or repeated while still needing separate evidence for truth, safety, or quality.

nodes.label: Standing Alone
nodes.full_label: Why Disagreement Feels Socially Risky | Logical Fallacies 998914 Bandwagon Pressure
nodes.catchy_title: Why Disagreement Feels Socially Risky
nodes.summary: People may publicly agree with a group because dissent feels embarrassing, isolating, or socially risky even when they privately doubt it.

nodes.label: Trending Loops
nodes.full_label: How Trending Numbers Create More Trending | Logical Fallacies 998914 Bandwagon Pressure
nodes.catchy_title: How Trending Numbers Create More Trending
nodes.summary: Ratings, follower counts, bestseller badges, and trending labels can help navigation while also making popularity feed on itself.

nodes.label: Circularity
nodes.full_label: Is the Argument Proving Itself? | Logical Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: Is the Argument Proving Itself?
nodes.summary: Circular reasoning restates the conclusion as support, leaving the real question unanswered.

nodes.label: Bible Loops
nodes.full_label: When Authority Arguments Turn in Circles | Logical Fallacies 998914 Circular Reasoning
nodes.catchy_title: When Authority Arguments Turn in Circles
nodes.summary: Religious authority arguments can become circular when a source is treated as true because the claim already assumes its truth.

nodes.label: Hidden Loops
nodes.full_label: How Long Argument Chains Hide Circularity | Logical Fallacies 998914 Circular Reasoning
nodes.catchy_title: How Long Argument Chains Hide Circularity
nodes.summary: Circular reasoning can be hard to spot when several claims form a chain that eventually loops back to the start.

nodes.label: News Trust
nodes.full_label: Can a Source Prove Its Own Reliability? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Circular Reasoning
nodes.catchy_title: Can a Source Prove Its Own Reliability?
nodes.summary: Media reliability claims become circular when accuracy is proved by trust and trust is proved by accuracy.

nodes.label: Rewording
nodes.full_label: When Explanations Just Rename the Claim | Logical Fallacies 998914 Circular Reasoning
nodes.catchy_title: When Explanations Just Rename the Claim
nodes.summary: Some explanations sound scientific while merely restating the thing they were meant to explain in different words.

nodes.label: Support Test
nodes.full_label: Would the Premise Convince a Skeptic? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Circular Reasoning
nodes.catchy_title: Would the Premise Convince a Skeptic?
nodes.summary: A simple test for circular reasoning is whether the premises could persuade someone who does not already accept the conclusion.

nodes.label: Context
nodes.full_label: When Is It Really a Fallacy? | Logical Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: When Is It Really a Fallacy?
nodes.summary: The same argument form can be reasonable in one setting and misleading in another because context changes the support.

nodes.label: Credibility
nodes.full_label: When Is Personal Criticism Relevant? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Borderline Context
nodes.catchy_title: When Is Personal Criticism Relevant?
nodes.summary: Personal criticism becomes relevant only when the person's credibility is part of the evidence being offered.

nodes.label: Expert Shortcuts
nodes.full_label: When Should You Trust an Expert? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Borderline Context
nodes.catchy_title: When Should You Trust an Expert?
nodes.summary: Expert opinion can be a reasonable shortcut when the authority is relevant, qualified, independent, and treated as defeasible.

nodes.label: Fear Warnings
nodes.full_label: When Is Fear a Fair Warning? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Borderline Context
nodes.catchy_title: When Is Fear a Fair Warning?
nodes.summary: Fear appeals are not automatically manipulative when the emotion points to a real danger and the conclusion stays proportionate.

nodes.label: No Proof
nodes.full_label: When Does No Proof Actually Matter? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Borderline Context
nodes.catchy_title: When Does No Proof Actually Matter?
nodes.summary: A lack of proof can be weak reasoning in science but decisive in law when one side carries the burden of proof.

nodes.label: Two Options
nodes.full_label: Are Those Really the Only Choices? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Borderline Context
nodes.catchy_title: Are Those Really the Only Choices?
nodes.summary: A two-option choice is fair only when the situation genuinely excludes compromise, delay, revision, or rival alternatives.

nodes.label: Deadlines
nodes.full_label: Will One Extension Ruin the Rules? | Logical Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: Will One Extension Ruin the Rules?
nodes.summary: Deadline arguments show how one exception can be framed as disaster without evidence for each later step.

nodes.label: Evidence Rules
nodes.full_label: What Proof Should an Extension Need? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Deadline Slippery
nodes.catchy_title: What Proof Should an Extension Need?
nodes.summary: Strong extension policies ask for enough evidence to verify hardship without turning every request into a punitive investigation.

nodes.label: Fairness Risk
nodes.full_label: When Does One Extension Become Unfair? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Deadline Slippery
nodes.catchy_title: When Does One Extension Become Unfair?
nodes.summary: A deadline extension is a real fairness risk when vague discretion, hidden decisions, or unequal access make similar cases come out differently.

nodes.label: Precedent
nodes.full_label: Does One Extension Force the Next? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Deadline Slippery
nodes.catchy_title: Does One Extension Force the Next?
nodes.summary: A past extension can guide future decisions without forcing every later request to receive the same answer.

nodes.label: Rule Limits
nodes.full_label: Is a Flexible Deadline Still a Deadline? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Deadline Slippery
nodes.catchy_title: Is a Flexible Deadline Still a Deadline?
nodes.summary: A rule does not stop being a rule just because it includes defined exceptions for emergencies or equal-access needs.

nodes.label: Self Certify
nodes.full_label: Can Self Certified Extensions Stay Fair? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Deadline Slippery
nodes.catchy_title: Can Self Certified Extensions Stay Fair?
nodes.summary: Limited self-certified extensions test whether simple safeguards can reduce abuse while helping people with short-term problems.

nodes.label: Debate
nodes.full_label: How to Spot Fallacies in Debate | Logical Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: How to Spot Fallacies in Debate
nodes.summary: Debates make fallacies tempting because speakers must answer quickly while persuading an audience.

nodes.label: Ad Hominem
nodes.full_label: Do Not Take the Personal Bait | Logical Fallacies 998914 Debate Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: Do Not Take the Personal Bait
nodes.summary: An ad hominem response should avoid the personality fight and bring attention back to the evidence at stake.

nodes.label: Charity
nodes.full_label: The Fairer Way to Win Arguments | Logical Fallacies 998914 Debate Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: The Fairer Way to Win Arguments
nodes.summary: Charitable reconstruction makes a rebuttal stronger by answering the best reasonable version of the opposing point.

nodes.label: False Choices
nodes.full_label: When Debate Choices Are Too Neat | Logical Fallacies 998914 Debate Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: When Debate Choices Are Too Neat
nodes.summary: False dilemmas can sound decisive because they turn a complex policy choice into only two visible options.

nodes.label: Labels
nodes.full_label: Should You Name the Fallacy? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Debate Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: Should You Name the Fallacy?
nodes.summary: A fallacy label helps only when the audience also hears exactly what reasoning step failed.

nodes.label: Straw Men
nodes.full_label: How to Answer a Straw Man Fast | Logical Fallacies 998914 Debate Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: How to Answer a Straw Man Fast
nodes.summary: A straw man rebuttal works best when it restores the real claim before explaining why the attack misses it.

nodes.label: Emotion
nodes.full_label: When Does Emotion Replace Evidence? | Logical Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: When Does Emotion Replace Evidence?
nodes.summary: Emotional appeals are not always fallacious, but they mislead when emotion substitutes for relevant support.

nodes.label: Fake News
nodes.full_label: Why Emotional Headlines Feel True | Logical Fallacies 998914 Appeal To Emotion
nodes.catchy_title: Why Emotional Headlines Feel True
nodes.summary: Emotional framing can make false headlines feel more believable when readers rely on feeling over checking.

nodes.label: Fake Urgency
nodes.full_label: How Countdown Pressure Shortens Judgment | Logical Fallacies 998914 Appeal To Emotion
nodes.catchy_title: How Countdown Pressure Shortens Judgment
nodes.summary: Countdowns, scarcity claims, and rushed prompts can pressure people to buy before they can inspect the reasons.

nodes.label: Fear Appeals
nodes.full_label: When Fear Warns but Does Not Prove | Logical Fallacies 998914 Appeal To Emotion
nodes.catchy_title: When Fear Warns but Does Not Prove
nodes.summary: Fear appeals are strongest when danger is real, but they become fallacious when fear is asked to prove a claim.

nodes.label: Pity Proof
nodes.full_label: When Pity Starts Doing the Proving | Logical Fallacies 998914 Appeal To Emotion
nodes.catchy_title: When Pity Starts Doing the Proving
nodes.summary: Appeal to pity goes wrong when real suffering is used to settle a factual question that still needs evidence.

nodes.label: Threats
nodes.full_label: Why Threats Are Not Evidence | Logical Fallacies 998914 Appeal To Emotion
nodes.catchy_title: Why Threats Are Not Evidence
nodes.summary: Threats may give people a reason to act, but they do not provide evidence that the threatened claim is true.

nodes.label: Equivocation
nodes.full_label: Did the Key Word Change Meaning? | Logical Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: Did the Key Word Change Meaning?
nodes.summary: Equivocation happens when an argument relies on a word changing meaning without making the shift clear.

nodes.label: Compare Fallacies
nodes.full_label: Which Ambiguity Fallacy Is Actually Happening? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Equivocation
nodes.catchy_title: Which Ambiguity Fallacy Is Actually Happening?
nodes.summary: Equivocation changes word meaning, amphiboly changes sentence structure and accent changes interpretation through emphasis.

nodes.label: Free Speech
nodes.full_label: When Does Free Speech Become a Word Game? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Equivocation
nodes.catchy_title: When Does Free Speech Become a Word Game?
nodes.summary: Arguments about free speech often blur legal protection, moral entitlement, social permission and immunity from criticism.

nodes.label: Natural Claims
nodes.full_label: Does Natural Really Mean Safe or Good? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Equivocation
nodes.catchy_title: Does Natural Really Mean Safe or Good?
nodes.summary: Calling something natural can shift from a description of origin into an unsupported claim about health, safety or value.

nodes.label: Spotting It
nodes.full_label: How Can You Tell When a Word Has Shifted? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Equivocation
nodes.catchy_title: How Can You Tell When a Word Has Shifted?
nodes.summary: A repeated word can make a weak argument look strong when its meaning quietly changes between premise and conclusion.

nodes.label: Theory Claims
nodes.full_label: Why Only a Theory Misleads About Science | Logical Fallacies 998914 Equivocation
nodes.catchy_title: Why Only a Theory Misleads About Science
nodes.summary: The phrase only a theory weakens science by judging a technical term as if it meant a casual guess.

nodes.label: Essays
nodes.full_label: How Fallacies Weaken Student Essays | Logical Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: How Fallacies Weaken Student Essays
nodes.summary: Fallacies in essays weaken credibility because the evidence does not connect cleanly to the thesis.

nodes.label: Because Gaps
nodes.full_label: When Because Does Not Prove the Point | Logical Fallacies 998914 Essay Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: When Because Does Not Prove the Point
nodes.summary: A weak because clause can make a paragraph sound persuasive while leaving the real proof missing.

nodes.label: Cherry Picking
nodes.full_label: The Evidence Your Essay Cannot Ignore | Logical Fallacies 998914 Essay Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: The Evidence Your Essay Cannot Ignore
nodes.summary: Ignoring the strongest contrary evidence can make an essay look selective even when many sources are cited.

nodes.label: Dropped Quotes
nodes.full_label: Why Quotations Cannot Argue Alone | Logical Fallacies 998914 Essay Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: Why Quotations Cannot Argue Alone
nodes.summary: A quotation only supports an essay claim when the writer explains what it shows and why it matters.

nodes.label: Scale Jumps
nodes.full_label: How One Example Becomes Too Much | Logical Fallacies 998914 Essay Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: How One Example Becomes Too Much
nodes.summary: One vivid example can be useful evidence, but it cannot carry a broad academic claim on its own.

nodes.label: Straw Men
nodes.full_label: Are You Answering the Real Objection? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Essay Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: Are You Answering the Real Objection?
nodes.summary: A counterargument becomes a straw man when it attacks a weaker version of an objection instead of the real one.

nodes.label: Evidence Gaps
nodes.full_label: What Evidence Is the Argument Missing? | Logical Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: What Evidence Is the Argument Missing?
nodes.summary: Many fallacies work by making thin or missing evidence feel stronger than it really is.

nodes.label: Ad Claims
nodes.full_label: What Should Ads Have to Prove? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Evidence Gaps
nodes.catchy_title: What Should Ads Have to Prove?
nodes.summary: Objective product claims need evidence strong enough to support both what is said and what consumers are likely to infer.

nodes.label: Anecdotes
nodes.full_label: Why One Story Feels Like a Pattern | Logical Fallacies 998914 Evidence Gaps
nodes.catchy_title: Why One Story Feels Like a Pattern
nodes.summary: A vivid story can prove something happened, but it cannot show how often it happens without wider evidence.

nodes.label: Bad Samples
nodes.full_label: When Five Voices Become Everyone | Logical Fallacies 998914 Evidence Gaps
nodes.catchy_title: When Five Voices Become Everyone
nodes.summary: A few easy-to-reach voices can reveal a real concern while still failing to show what most people think.

nodes.label: Cherry Picking
nodes.full_label: When One Study Hides the Rest | Logical Fallacies 998914 Evidence Gaps
nodes.catchy_title: When One Study Hides the Rest
nodes.summary: A single favorable study can mislead when stronger, larger, or contradictory evidence is left out.

nodes.label: False Cause
nodes.full_label: Did It Work, Or Just Happen After? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Evidence Gaps
nodes.catchy_title: Did It Work, Or Just Happen After?
nodes.summary: Improvement after a change is not enough to prove the change caused it unless rival explanations are addressed.

nodes.label: False Cause
nodes.full_label: Did One Thing Really Cause Another? | Logical Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: Did One Thing Really Cause Another?
nodes.summary: Post hoc reasoning mistakes sequence for causation when other explanations may fit the same events.

nodes.label: Counterfactuals
nodes.full_label: The One Question False Causes Avoid | Logical Fallacies 998914 Post Hoc Reasoning
nodes.catchy_title: The One Question False Causes Avoid
nodes.summary: Asking what probably would have happened without the supposed cause helps reveal whether timing is doing too much work.

nodes.label: Lucky Rituals
nodes.full_label: Why Lucky Shirts Feel Like Evidence | Logical Fallacies 998914 Post Hoc Reasoning
nodes.catchy_title: Why Lucky Shirts Feel Like Evidence
nodes.summary: Superstitions often grow from memorable sequences where a personal ritual is mistaken for influence over chance outcomes.

nodes.label: Policy Timing
nodes.full_label: Did the Policy Work, or Just Arrive First? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Post Hoc Reasoning
nodes.catchy_title: Did the Policy Work, or Just Arrive First?
nodes.summary: A policy followed by better outcomes may deserve attention, but background trends and other changes can explain the same result.

nodes.label: Regression
nodes.full_label: When Improvement Was Already Likely | Logical Fallacies 998914 Post Hoc Reasoning
nodes.catchy_title: When Improvement Was Already Likely
nodes.summary: Extreme results often move closer to normal on their own, making weak interventions look more effective than they are.

nodes.label: VAERS Reports
nodes.full_label: When After a Vaccine Is Not Proof | Logical Fallacies 998914 Post Hoc Reasoning
nodes.catchy_title: When After a Vaccine Is Not Proof
nodes.summary: Reports after vaccination can flag safety questions, but timing alone does not show that a vaccine caused the event.

nodes.label: False Dilemma
nodes.full_label: What Choices Are Being Hidden? | Logical Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: What Choices Are Being Hidden?
nodes.summary: False dilemmas make complex choices look like only two extremes when practical alternatives may exist.

nodes.label: Budget Debates
nodes.full_label: Is It Really Pay More or Collapse? | Logical Fallacies 998914 False Dilemmas
nodes.catchy_title: Is It Really Pay More or Collapse?
nodes.summary: Budget claims like raise prices or face ruin often hide implementation choices about spending, timing, reserves, and safeguards.

nodes.label: Bush Phrase
nodes.full_label: What Did 'With US' Leave Out? | Logical Fallacies 998914 False Dilemmas
nodes.catchy_title: What Did 'With US' Leave Out?
nodes.summary: The post-9/11 phrase shows how political rhetoric can draw a sharp boundary while obscuring disagreement over methods.

nodes.label: Privacy Security
nodes.full_label: Do We Have to Choose Privacy or Safety? | Logical Fallacies 998914 False Dilemmas
nodes.catchy_title: Do We Have to Choose Privacy or Safety?
nodes.summary: Privacy and security can conflict, but warrants, oversight, audits, and narrower rules show why the choice is rarely absolute.

nodes.label: Real Choices
nodes.full_label: When Is a Dilemma Actually Real? | Logical Fallacies 998914 False Dilemmas
nodes.catchy_title: When Is a Dilemma Actually Real?
nodes.summary: Some decisions really do narrow to two choices, but the surrounding causes and remedies may still be more complex.

nodes.label: Spotting Gaps
nodes.full_label: What Options Did the Argument Leave Out? | Logical Fallacies 998914 False Dilemmas
nodes.catchy_title: What Options Did the Argument Leave Out?
nodes.summary: Either-or claims become easier to test when you separate the offered choice from the practical options left out.

nodes.label: Formal Logic
nodes.full_label: When the Structure Makes Reasoning Fail | Logical Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: When the Structure Makes Reasoning Fail
nodes.summary: Formal fallacies show how an argument can fail even when its individual statements sound plausible.

nodes.label: Existence Errors
nodes.full_label: Do Universal Claims Prove Anything Exists | Logical Fallacies 998914 Formal Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: Do Universal Claims Prove Anything Exists
nodes.summary: A statement about all members of a category may say nothing about whether that category has any real members.

nodes.label: False Effects
nodes.full_label: When Evidence Looks Like Proof but Isnt | Logical Fallacies 998914 Formal Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: When Evidence Looks Like Proof but Isnt
nodes.summary: A matching effect can support a hypothesis, but it does not deductively prove the one cause you already had in mind.

nodes.label: Other Causes
nodes.full_label: The Fallacy That Rules Out Too Much | Logical Fallacies 998914 Formal Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: The Fallacy That Rules Out Too Much
nodes.summary: The absence of one sufficient condition does not prove that the expected result cannot happen another way.

nodes.label: Probability Trap
nodes.full_label: When Rare Evidence Misleads a Jury | Logical Fallacies 998914 Formal Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: When Rare Evidence Misleads a Jury
nodes.summary: Rare evidence can be powerful, but reversing the probability question can make it seem far more conclusive than it is.

nodes.label: Shared Category
nodes.full_label: Why Shared Traits Do Not Prove Identity | Logical Fallacies 998914 Formal Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: Why Shared Traits Do Not Prove Identity
nodes.summary: Two things can share a broad category without being identical, equivalent, or logically connected in the claimed way.

nodes.label: Ignorance
nodes.full_label: What Does Missing Evidence Prove? | Logical Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: What Does Missing Evidence Prove?
nodes.summary: Appeal to ignorance turns a gap in evidence into proof unless the missing evidence would reasonably be expected.

nodes.label: Not Proven
nodes.full_label: Why Not Guilty Is Not the Same as False | Logical Fallacies 998914 Appeal To Ignorance
nodes.catchy_title: Why Not Guilty Is Not the Same as False
nodes.summary: A legal acquittal means guilt was not proved under the required standard, not that every factual question is settled.

nodes.label: Null Results
nodes.full_label: When No Effect Has Not Been Proved | Logical Fallacies 998914 Appeal To Ignorance
nodes.catchy_title: When No Effect Has Not Been Proved
nodes.summary: A study can fail to find an effect because the effect is absent, or because the test was too small or too noisy to detect it.

nodes.label: Proof Burden
nodes.full_label: Who Has to Prove the Claim? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Appeal To Ignorance
nodes.catchy_title: Who Has to Prove the Claim?
nodes.summary: The person making a claim cannot make it true by demanding that everyone else disprove it first.

nodes.label: Rumour Gaps
nodes.full_label: Why Silence Makes Rumours Feel True | Logical Fallacies 998914 Appeal To Ignorance
nodes.catchy_title: Why Silence Makes Rumours Feel True
nodes.summary: A delayed or absent denial can raise questions, but it does not by itself confirm that a rumour is true.

nodes.label: Silence Test
nodes.full_label: When Does No Evidence Actually Count? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Appeal To Ignorance
nodes.catchy_title: When Does No Evidence Actually Count?
nodes.summary: A missing trace matters only when the claim would normally leave evidence that a fair search could find.

nodes.label: Informal Logic
nodes.full_label: Why Context Changes the Argument | Logical Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: Why Context Changes the Argument
nodes.summary: Informal fallacies depend on context, wording, relevance and evidence rather than a fixed logical form.

nodes.label: Ad Hominem
nodes.full_label: When Personal Criticism Actually Matters | Logical Fallacies 998914 Informal Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: When Personal Criticism Actually Matters
nodes.summary: Criticising a person is not automatically fallacious; the question is whether the criticism affects the claim.

nodes.label: Anecdotes
nodes.full_label: When One Story Becomes Too Much Proof | Logical Fallacies 998914 Informal Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: When One Story Becomes Too Much Proof
nodes.summary: Personal experience can be useful evidence, but it often cannot carry a broad conclusion by itself.

nodes.label: Authority
nodes.full_label: When Expert Opinion Is Not Enough | Logical Fallacies 998914 Informal Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: When Expert Opinion Is Not Enough
nodes.summary: Expert opinion can support a claim, but it should not replace evidence or hide uncertainty.

nodes.label: Equivocation
nodes.full_label: When One Word Quietly Changes the Argument | Logical Fallacies 998914 Informal Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: When One Word Quietly Changes the Argument
nodes.summary: A small change in meaning can make a weak argument look much stronger than it is.

nodes.label: Red Herrings
nodes.full_label: Is That Point Relevant or a Distraction? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Informal Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: Is That Point Relevant or a Distraction?
nodes.summary: A vivid side issue can feel persuasive while leaving the original claim unanswered.

nodes.label: Labels
nodes.full_label: When Fallacy Labels Mislead Too | Logical Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: When Fallacy Labels Mislead Too
nodes.summary: Calling something a fallacy does not prove its conclusion false or end the need for analysis.

nodes.label: Anecdotes
nodes.full_label: Does Anecdotal Evidence Make a Claim False? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Fallacy Labels
nodes.catchy_title: Does Anecdotal Evidence Make a Claim False?
nodes.summary: Anecdotes can be weak evidence, but dismissing the conclusion solely because the story is anecdotal repeats the error in reverse.

nodes.label: Authority
nodes.full_label: When Expert Authority Is Helpful or Misleading | Logical Fallacies 998914 Fallacy Labels
nodes.catchy_title: When Expert Authority Is Helpful or Misleading
nodes.summary: Appeals to authority need checks for expertise, accuracy, independence, and evidence before they deserve trust.

nodes.label: Bad vs True
nodes.full_label: When Bad Arguments Still Reach True Claims | Logical Fallacies 998914 Fallacy Labels
nodes.catchy_title: When Bad Arguments Still Reach True Claims
nodes.summary: A bad reason can fail to prove a claim without making the opposite claim true.

nodes.label: Callouts
nodes.full_label: Why Online Fallacy Callouts Go Wrong | Logical Fallacies 998914 Fallacy Labels
nodes.catchy_title: Why Online Fallacy Callouts Go Wrong
nodes.summary: Online fallacy callouts can clarify a thread, but they often become quick dismissal instead of real evidence-checking.

nodes.label: Repair
nodes.full_label: How Fallacy Labels Can Improve Arguments | Logical Fallacies 998914 Fallacy Labels
nodes.catchy_title: How Fallacy Labels Can Improve Arguments
nodes.summary: Fallacy labels work best when they help writers revise weak support rather than punish them for making a mistake.

nodes.label: Loaded Words
nodes.full_label: What Is the Wording Sneaking In? | Logical Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: What Is the Wording Sneaking In?
nodes.summary: Loaded wording can smuggle assumptions into an argument before the evidence has been examined.

nodes.label: Biased Surveys
nodes.full_label: How Question Wording Skews Survey Results | Logical Fallacies 998914 Loaded Language
nodes.catchy_title: How Question Wording Skews Survey Results
nodes.summary: Question wording can distort survey results by assuming facts, steering responses or narrowing acceptable choices.

nodes.label: Charged Labels
nodes.full_label: Are the Labels Doing More Than the Evidence? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Loaded Language
nodes.catchy_title: Are the Labels Doing More Than the Evidence?
nodes.summary: Words such as 'corrupt', 'humane' or 'reckless' can push a conclusion before the supporting facts are established.

nodes.label: Hidden Assumptions
nodes.full_label: How to Detect the Premises No One Defends | Logical Fallacies 998914 Loaded Language
nodes.catchy_title: How to Detect the Premises No One Defends
nodes.summary: A few diagnostic questions can reveal whether an argument depends on an unsupported background assumption.

nodes.label: Loaded Questions
nodes.full_label: When Does a Question Smuggle In an Answer? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Loaded Language
nodes.catchy_title: When Does a Question Smuggle In an Answer?
nodes.summary: Some questions are structured so that any direct answer appears to accept a claim that has never been proven.

nodes.label: Memory Framing
nodes.full_label: Can One Word Change What People Remember? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Loaded Language
nodes.catchy_title: Can One Word Change What People Remember?
nodes.summary: Small wording changes in questions can alter what people recall and report about the same event.

nodes.label: No True
nodes.full_label: Are Definitions Moving to Escape Evidence? | Logical Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: Are Definitions Moving to Escape Evidence?
nodes.summary: The no true Scotsman move protects a general claim by redefining membership whenever counterexamples appear.

nodes.label: Fair Redefinition
nodes.full_label: When Is Redefinition Not a Fallacy? | Logical Fallacies 998914 No True Scotsman
nodes.catchy_title: When Is Redefinition Not a Fallacy?
nodes.summary: Some exclusions are not evasions because the boundary is built into law, credentials, rules, or ordinary usage.

nodes.label: Membership Tests
nodes.full_label: When Does a True Member Really Count? | Logical Fallacies 998914 No True Scotsman
nodes.catchy_title: When Does a True Member Really Count?
nodes.summary: A membership claim becomes fairer when its rule is stated in advance, applied consistently, and open to real counterexamples.

nodes.label: Persuasive Words
nodes.full_label: When Definitions Carry Hidden Judgment | Logical Fallacies 998914 No True Scotsman
nodes.catchy_title: When Definitions Carry Hidden Judgment
nodes.summary: A familiar praise word can keep its emotional appeal while its boundary quietly changes to favor one side.

nodes.label: Porridge Case
nodes.full_label: Why the Porridge Example Still Works | Logical Fallacies 998914 No True Scotsman
nodes.catchy_title: Why the Porridge Example Still Works
nodes.summary: The porridge story shows how one word, true, can turn a testable claim into a protected identity label.

nodes.label: Purity Labels
nodes.full_label: How Purity Labels Shut Down Evidence | Logical Fallacies 998914 No True Scotsman
nodes.catchy_title: How Purity Labels Shut Down Evidence
nodes.summary: Words like real, genuine, and proper can police identity instead of answering evidence.

nodes.label: Novelty
nodes.full_label: Is New Always Better? | Logical Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: Is New Always Better?
nodes.summary: Appeal to novelty assumes newer ideas, tools or policies are better simply because they are recent.

nodes.label: Fair Comparison
nodes.full_label: How to Compare Old and New Fairly | Logical Fallacies 998914 Appeal To Novelty
nodes.catchy_title: How to Compare Old and New Fairly
nodes.summary: The fair test is not whether an option is old or new, but what each one improves, preserves, risks, and costs.

nodes.label: Medical Proof
nodes.full_label: When New Treatments Outrun the Evidence | Logical Fallacies 998914 Appeal To Novelty
nodes.catchy_title: When New Treatments Outrun the Evidence
nodes.summary: A new treatment can be promising without yet proving that it helps patients more than existing care.

nodes.label: Modern Claims
nodes.full_label: When Modern Language Does the Persuading | Logical Fallacies 998914 Appeal To Novelty
nodes.catchy_title: When Modern Language Does the Persuading
nodes.summary: Calling a reform modern can make it sound progressive before anyone proves that it improves outcomes.

nodes.label: New Coke
nodes.full_label: Why New Coke Was Not Just a Taste Test | Logical Fallacies 998914 Appeal To Novelty
nodes.catchy_title: Why New Coke Was Not Just a Taste Test
nodes.summary: New Coke shows how a tested improvement can still fail when it misses what people valued in the old product.

nodes.label: Tech Hype
nodes.full_label: Does the New Feature Still Work Later? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Appeal To Novelty
nodes.catchy_title: Does the New Feature Still Work Later?
nodes.summary: A new feature can look successful at launch because users are curious, not because the change will keep working.

nodes.label: Phones
nodes.full_label: Are Phone Rules Really All or Nothing? | Logical Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: Are Phone Rules Really All or Nothing?
nodes.summary: School phone debates show how false dilemmas can hide practical middle-ground policy options.

nodes.label: Ban Models
nodes.full_label: What Does a Phone Ban Actually Mean? | Logical Fallacies 998914 School Phone Policy
nodes.catchy_title: What Does a Phone Ban Actually Mean?
nodes.summary: A phone-free day can be stricter than classroom limits without requiring every pupil to leave their device at home.

nodes.label: Exceptions
nodes.full_label: When Should a Phone Rule Bend? | Logical Fallacies 998914 School Phone Policy
nodes.catchy_title: When Should a Phone Rule Bend?
nodes.summary: Exceptions for health, disability, caring and safety needs can make a strict rule fairer without making it meaningless.

nodes.label: Locked Pouches
nodes.full_label: Are Locked Pouches a Simple Fix? | Logical Fallacies 998914 School Phone Policy
nodes.catchy_title: Are Locked Pouches a Simple Fix?
nodes.summary: Locked pouches reduce access during school, but they can also bring costs, resistance and new discipline problems.

nodes.label: Test Scores
nodes.full_label: Do Phone Bans Raise Test Scores? | Logical Fallacies 998914 School Phone Policy
nodes.catchy_title: Do Phone Bans Raise Test Scores?
nodes.summary: One influential English study found test-score gains from bans, especially for lower-achieving pupils, but it cannot settle every policy question.

nodes.label: Wellbeing
nodes.full_label: Do Phone Rules Improve Wellbeing? | Logical Fallacies 998914 School Phone Policy
nodes.catchy_title: Do Phone Rules Improve Wellbeing?
nodes.summary: Restricting phones can reduce school-day use, but current evidence does not prove broad improvements in wellbeing, sleep or anxiety.

nodes.label: Politics
nodes.full_label: How Public Arguments Go Off Track | Logical Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: How Public Arguments Go Off Track
nodes.summary: Political arguments often mix emotion, identity and evidence, making relevance and support especially important.

nodes.label: Ad Hominem
nodes.full_label: When Personal Attacks Hide the Policy Question | Logical Fallacies 998914 Political Speech Fal
nodes.catchy_title: When Personal Attacks Hide the Policy Question
nodes.summary: Personal attacks can make opponents seem illegitimate while leaving the policy question itself unanswered.

nodes.label: Deregulation
nodes.full_label: The Missing Middle in Deregulation Debates | Logical Fallacies 998914 Political Speech Fal
nodes.catchy_title: The Missing Middle in Deregulation Debates
nodes.summary: Deregulation claims can turn a spectrum of policy choices into a forced choice between freedom and collapse.

nodes.label: Polite Fallacies
nodes.full_label: Can a Fallacy Sound Perfectly Reasonable? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Political Speech Fal
nodes.catchy_title: Can a Fallacy Sound Perfectly Reasonable?
nodes.summary: Fallacious arguments can sound civil and reasonable while still steering audiences away from evidence.

nodes.label: Popularity
nodes.full_label: When Majority Support Becomes Fake Proof | Logical Fallacies 998914 Political Speech Fal
nodes.catchy_title: When Majority Support Becomes Fake Proof
nodes.summary: Majority support can be politically important, but it does not prove that a claim is true or a policy is sound.

nodes.label: Straw Man
nodes.full_label: How Healthcare Claims Become Straw Men | Logical Fallacies 998914 Political Speech Fal
nodes.catchy_title: How Healthcare Claims Become Straw Men
nodes.summary: Healthcare arguments can become easier to attack when a complex proposal is recast as a frightening caricature.

nodes.label: Popularity
nodes.full_label: Does Belief Make a Claim True? | Logical Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: Does Belief Make a Claim True?
nodes.summary: Appeal to popularity treats widespread belief as proof, even though popularity and truth are different questions.

nodes.label: Cascades
nodes.full_label: How Bandwagons Grow From Thin Evidence | Logical Fallacies 998914 Appeal To Popularity
nodes.catchy_title: How Bandwagons Grow From Thin Evidence
nodes.summary: Information cascades explain how early public choices can drown out later private evidence and make a weak crowd look informed.

nodes.label: Fake Reviews
nodes.full_label: Can Popular Reviews Be Trusted? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Appeal To Popularity
nodes.catchy_title: Can Popular Reviews Be Trusted?
nodes.summary: Ratings and reviews can guide choices, but fake reviews create artificial crowd belief that looks more evidential than it is.

nodes.label: Popularity Bias
nodes.full_label: Why Trending Lists Can Distort Judgment | Logical Fallacies 998914 Appeal To Popularity
nodes.catchy_title: Why Trending Lists Can Distort Judgment
nodes.summary: Recommendation platforms can make already-popular items more visible, turning exposure into a feedback loop that feels like proof.

nodes.label: Social Proof
nodes.full_label: When Social Proof Stops Being Evidence | Logical Fallacies 998914 Appeal To Popularity
nodes.catchy_title: When Social Proof Stops Being Evidence
nodes.summary: Crowd behavior can be useful under uncertainty, but it becomes risky when imitation is mistaken for independent proof.

nodes.label: The Asch Conformity Experiments
nodes.full_label: Why Obvious Answers Can Bend Under Pressure | Logical Fallacies 998914 Appeal To Popularity
nodes.catchy_title: Why Obvious Answers Can Bend Under Pressure
nodes.summary: The Asch line studies show how group agreement can push people toward answers that conflict with what they can see.

nodes.label: Red Herring
nodes.full_label: Is This Point Actually Relevant? | Logical Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: Is This Point Actually Relevant?
nodes.summary: Red herrings introduce interesting but irrelevant material that avoids the question being asked.

nodes.label: Context Test
nodes.full_label: Is It Context or a Dodge? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Red Herrings
nodes.catchy_title: Is It Context or a Dodge?
nodes.summary: Context is useful only when it helps answer the original question instead of replacing it with an easier one.

nodes.label: Dead Cat
nodes.full_label: Why Shocking Distractions Work | Logical Fallacies 998914 Red Herrings
nodes.catchy_title: Why Shocking Distractions Work
nodes.summary: A shocking new topic can dominate attention even when observers recognize that it has not answered the damaging question.

nodes.label: Detail Flood
nodes.full_label: When Details Become a Smokescreen | Logical Fallacies 998914 Red Herrings
nodes.catchy_title: When Details Become a Smokescreen
nodes.summary: Too many details can feel like evidence while actually burying the question that needed a clear answer.

nodes.label: Straw Man
nodes.full_label: Straw Man or Red Herring? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Red Herrings
nodes.catchy_title: Straw Man or Red Herring?
nodes.summary: A straw man attacks a distorted claim, while a red herring leaves the original claim behind without necessarily misrepresenting it.

nodes.label: Whataboutism
nodes.full_label: When Whataboutism Becomes a Dodge | Logical Fallacies 998914 Red Herrings
nodes.catchy_title: When Whataboutism Becomes a Dodge
nodes.summary: Whataboutism can expose real double standards, but it becomes a diversion when it avoids the charge on the table.

nodes.label: Relevance
nodes.full_label: Does This Reason Actually Matter? | Logical Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: Does This Reason Actually Matter?
nodes.summary: Relevance tests ask whether a reason actually bears on the conclusion rather than merely sounding persuasive.

nodes.label: Ad Hominem
nodes.full_label: When Character Attacks Are Actually Relevant | Logical Fallacies 998914 Relevance Tests
nodes.catchy_title: When Character Attacks Are Actually Relevant
nodes.summary: Personal criticism matters only when the conclusion depends on trustworthiness, testimony or conflicts of interest.

nodes.label: Pity Appeals
nodes.full_label: When Sympathy Does Not Prove the Claim | Logical Fallacies 998914 Relevance Tests
nodes.catchy_title: When Sympathy Does Not Prove the Claim
nodes.summary: Hardship may deserve compassion, but it does not automatically prove that a grade has been earned.

nodes.label: Popularity
nodes.full_label: Does Popular Belief Make a Claim True? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Relevance Tests
nodes.catchy_title: Does Popular Belief Make a Claim True?
nodes.summary: Majority belief can show what people think, but it rarely proves that a factual, moral or historical claim is true.

nodes.label: Red Herrings
nodes.full_label: When True Concerns Pull Arguments Off Track | Logical Fallacies 998914 Relevance Tests
nodes.catchy_title: When True Concerns Pull Arguments Off Track
nodes.summary: A real concern can still distract when it answers a different question from the one being argued.

nodes.label: Warrants
nodes.full_label: The Missing Bridge Between Evidence and Claim | Logical Fallacies 998914 Relevance Tests
nodes.catchy_title: The Missing Bridge Between Evidence and Claim
nodes.summary: The warrant is the missing bridge that explains why a reason actually supports a conclusion.

nodes.label: Remedies
nodes.full_label: Do Popular Remedies Prove Themselves? | Logical Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: Do Popular Remedies Prove Themselves?
nodes.summary: Claims about remedies often confuse popularity, anecdotes and missing disproof with reliable evidence.

nodes.label: Ad Red Flags
nodes.full_label: How miracle cure ads sell belief | Logical Fallacies 998914 Health Claim Fallaci
nodes.catchy_title: How miracle cure ads sell belief
nodes.summary: Miracle-cure ads often repeat recognizable warning signs, from secret ingredients to conspiracy claims about suppressed cures.

nodes.label: FDA Warnings
nodes.full_label: What warning databases reveal about remedies | Logical Fallacies 998914 Health Claim Fallaci
nodes.catchy_title: What warning databases reveal about remedies
nodes.summary: Regulatory warning lists show that products can be marketed and bought before their claims or ingredients are trustworthy.

nodes.label: Interactions
nodes.full_label: Natural does not always mean safe | Logical Fallacies 998914 Health Claim Fallaci
nodes.catchy_title: Natural does not always mean safe
nodes.summary: Natural products can have real biological effects, including interactions that weaken or intensify prescribed medicines.

nodes.label: Popularity
nodes.full_label: Why bestsellers can still mislead | Logical Fallacies 998914 Health Claim Fallaci
nodes.catchy_title: Why bestsellers can still mislead
nodes.summary: A bestseller label or millions of users can show demand, but it cannot prove that a product treats disease.

nodes.label: Testimonials
nodes.full_label: When recovery stories are not evidence | Logical Fallacies 998914 Health Claim Fallaci
nodes.catchy_title: When recovery stories are not evidence
nodes.summary: Personal recovery stories can be sincere and still fail to show whether a remedy caused the improvement.

nodes.label: Rumours
nodes.full_label: Why Rumours Feel Like Evidence | Logical Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: Why Rumours Feel Like Evidence
nodes.summary: Rumours often rely on ignorance, popularity or weak causal links instead of verifiable support.

nodes.label: False Cause
nodes.full_label: Did that really cause this? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Rumour Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: Did that really cause this?
nodes.summary: A rumour can feel explanatory when it links two events by timing, but sequence alone does not prove cause.

nodes.label: FOAF Claims
nodes.full_label: Who actually said the warning? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Rumour Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: Who actually said the warning?
nodes.summary: Anonymous experts and distant personal connections can lend rumours borrowed credibility without real accountability.

nodes.label: Health Harm
nodes.full_label: When health rumours become dangerous | Logical Fallacies 998914 Rumour Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: When health rumours become dangerous
nodes.summary: Health rumours can move from weak reasoning to dangerous action when fear, false causes, and trusted messengers combine.

nodes.label: No Disproof
nodes.full_label: Why no disproof is not proof | Logical Fallacies 998914 Rumour Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: Why no disproof is not proof
nodes.summary: A claim does not become credible just because critics have not disproved every possible version of it.

nodes.label: Viral Proof
nodes.full_label: When sharing looks like evidence | Logical Fallacies 998914 Rumour Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: When sharing looks like evidence
nodes.summary: Many reposts can look like many witnesses, even when they all trace back to the same unverified source.

nodes.label: Safety Claims
nodes.full_label: Did the Answer Address Safety? | Logical Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: Did the Answer Address Safety?
nodes.summary: Corporate responses can dodge safety questions by shifting attention to unrelated good deeds or brand messages.

nodes.label: CPSC Reporting
nodes.full_label: Why Regulators Want Hazard Facts Fast | Logical Fallacies 998914 Product Safety Red
nodes.catchy_title: Why Regulators Want Hazard Facts Fast
nodes.summary: Hazard-reporting duties make the core question practical: what did the company know, when did it report, and what should users do now?

nodes.label: Crash Stats
nodes.full_label: When Safety Statistics Compare the Wrong Things | Logical Fallacies 998914 Product Safety Red
nodes.catchy_title: When Safety Statistics Compare the Wrong Things
nodes.summary: A favorable safety statistic can mislead when the comparison groups do not measure the same kind of crash or driving condition.

nodes.label: Safety Pledges
nodes.full_label: When 'We Care About Safety' Is Not an Answer | Logical Fallacies 998914 Product Safety Red
nodes.catchy_title: When 'We Care About Safety' Is Not an Answer
nodes.summary: A safety pledge only answers a product hazard claim when it is tied to incidents, testing, user advice, and corrective action.

nodes.label: Scale Claims
nodes.full_label: Can Big Numbers Hide a Serious Hazard? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Product Safety Red
nodes.catchy_title: Can Big Numbers Hide a Serious Hazard?
nodes.summary: Millions of successful uses can still leave a small exposed group facing an unacceptable product risk.

nodes.label: Tread Case
nodes.full_label: Did Warnings Answer the Tread+ Risk? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Product Safety Red
nodes.catchy_title: Did Warnings Answer the Tread+ Risk?
nodes.summary: The Tread+ dispute shows why blaming unsafe use can miss design risks in ordinary homes with children, pets, and distractions.

nodes.label: Slippery Slope
nodes.full_label: Will One Step Really Lead There? | Logical Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: Will One Step Really Lead There?
nodes.summary: Slippery slope arguments need evidence that each step in the predicted chain is likely, not just possible.

nodes.label: Boundaries
nodes.full_label: Does a Blurry Line Mean No Line? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Slippery Slope
nodes.catchy_title: Does a Blurry Line Mean No Line?
nodes.summary: Blurred boundaries can make decisions harder, but they do not prove that every practical distinction is arbitrary.

nodes.label: Mechanisms
nodes.full_label: What Actually Makes the Slope Slippery? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Slippery Slope
nodes.catchy_title: What Actually Makes the Slope Slippery?
nodes.summary: A stronger warning explains the mechanism that could make later steps easier after the first decision.

nodes.label: Missing Middle
nodes.full_label: Where Did the Middle of the Slope Go? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Slippery Slope
nodes.catchy_title: Where Did the Middle of the Slope Go?
nodes.summary: A slippery slope warning fails when it jumps from a modest first step to a frightening endpoint without showing the steps between.

nodes.label: Precedent
nodes.full_label: Does One Exception Really Rewrite the Rule? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Slippery Slope
nodes.catchy_title: Does One Exception Really Rewrite the Rule?
nodes.summary: Precedent matters, but one decision does not automatically force every later case to be treated the same way.

nodes.label: Safeguards
nodes.full_label: Can the Slide Be Stopped in Time? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Slippery Slope
nodes.catchy_title: Can the Slide Be Stopped in Time?
nodes.summary: A risk argument is stronger when it explains why safeguards might fail, and weaker when it ignores safeguards that could work.

nodes.label: Social Media
nodes.full_label: Why Bad Arguments Spread Fast Online | Logical Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: Why Bad Arguments Spread Fast Online
nodes.summary: Social media can reward quick, emotional and simplified arguments before their reasoning is checked.

nodes.label: False Choices
nodes.full_label: When Viral Posts Force False Choices | Logical Fallacies 998914 Social Media Fallaci
nodes.catchy_title: When Viral Posts Force False Choices
nodes.summary: Viral claims often flatten messy issues into two-sided moral tests that hide missing evidence and reasonable nuance.

nodes.label: False News
nodes.full_label: Why False Claims Outrun Careful Corrections | Logical Fallacies 998914 Social Media Fallaci
nodes.catchy_title: Why False Claims Outrun Careful Corrections
nodes.summary: False claims often travel farther than careful corrections because novelty, speed and social sharing reward simple stories.

nodes.label: Outrage
nodes.full_label: Does Outrage Make Bad Arguments Spread? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Social Media Fallaci
nodes.catchy_title: Does Outrage Make Bad Arguments Spread?
nodes.summary: Outrage can draw attention to real harms, but it becomes risky when emotional force substitutes for valid reasoning.

nodes.label: Pile Ons
nodes.full_label: When Personal Attacks Pretend To Prove A Point | Logical Fallacies 998914 Social Media Fallaci
nodes.catchy_title: When Personal Attacks Pretend To Prove A Point
nodes.summary: Personal attacks can feel like decisive answers online while leaving the actual claim and evidence untouched.

nodes.label: Screenshots
nodes.full_label: Why Screenshots Are Not Always Evidence | Logical Fallacies 998914 Social Media Fallaci
nodes.catchy_title: Why Screenshots Are Not Always Evidence
nodes.summary: A real screenshot, quote or personal story can still support a bad conclusion when context and scale are missing.

nodes.label: Sports Cause
nodes.full_label: Did the Logo Cause the Losing Streak? | Logical Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: Did the Logo Cause the Losing Streak?
nodes.summary: Sports superstitions show how timing can be mistaken for cause when performance has many possible explanations.

nodes.label: Evidence Checks
nodes.full_label: How to Test a Sports Logo Curse | Logical Fallacies 998914 Sports False Cause
nodes.catchy_title: How to Test a Sports Logo Curse
nodes.summary: A serious logo-causation claim needs competing explanations, performance data and a clear path from symbol to results.

nodes.label: Fan Backlash
nodes.full_label: Why New Sports Logos Make Fans Angry | Logical Fallacies 998914 Sports False Cause
nodes.catchy_title: Why New Sports Logos Make Fans Angry
nodes.summary: A rebrand can damage trust, identity and merchandise appeal even when it does not directly explain on-field results.

nodes.label: Logo Rules
nodes.full_label: Respect Ritual or Real Sports Curse? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Sports False Cause
nodes.catchy_title: Respect Ritual or Real Sports Curse?
nodes.summary: Avoiding the dressing-room logo can be a meaningful team norm without proving that stepping on it changes the score.

nodes.label: Lucky Hits
nodes.full_label: Why Logo Superstitions Survive Bad Evidence | Logical Fallacies 998914 Sports False Cause
nodes.catchy_title: Why Logo Superstitions Survive Bad Evidence
nodes.summary: Logo superstitions survive because remembered hits, forgotten misses and revised rituals make them hard to disprove.

nodes.label: Post Hoc
nodes.full_label: Did the Logo Really Cause the Losing Streak? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Sports False Cause
nodes.catchy_title: Did the Logo Really Cause the Losing Streak?
nodes.summary: A losing streak after a crest change can feel like proof, but timing alone cannot show that the badge caused the slump.

nodes.label: Straw Man
nodes.full_label: Are You Answering the Real Argument? | Logical Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: Are You Answering the Real Argument?
nodes.summary: A straw man replaces a real position with an easier target, making disagreement look simpler than it is.

nodes.label: Corrections
nodes.full_label: How to Answer a Straw Man | Logical Fallacies 998914 Straw Man Arguments
nodes.catchy_title: How to Answer a Straw Man
nodes.summary: A good correction identifies the changed claim, restores the real target and returns the discussion to the evidence.

nodes.label: Exaggeration
nodes.full_label: When Moderate Claims Become Easy Targets | Logical Fallacies 998914 Straw Man Arguments
nodes.catchy_title: When Moderate Claims Become Easy Targets
nodes.summary: Exaggeration makes careful proposals easier to attack by replacing limits, trade-offs and qualifications with an extreme version.

nodes.label: Hollow Men
nodes.full_label: Who Actually Holds That View? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Straw Man Arguments
nodes.catchy_title: Who Actually Holds That View?
nodes.summary: Hollow man arguments attack unnamed critics or generic groups in ways that make the target hard to verify.

nodes.label: Quote Mining
nodes.full_label: How Quotes Lose Their Meaning | Logical Fallacies 998914 Straw Man Arguments
nodes.catchy_title: How Quotes Lose Their Meaning
nodes.summary: Selective quotation can make a speaker sound simpler, harsher or more extreme than the full passage supports.

nodes.label: Weak Manning
nodes.full_label: When the Weakest Example Stands In | Logical Fallacies 998914 Straw Man Arguments
nodes.catchy_title: When the Weakest Example Stands In
nodes.summary: Weak-manning lets an arguer defeat a poor example of a view while implying that the stronger side has no serious case.

nodes.label: Tone
nodes.full_label: Is Tone the Same as Logic? | Logical Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: Is Tone the Same as Logic?
nodes.summary: An argument can be impolite yet relevant, or polite yet logically weak, so tone alone is not the test.

nodes.label: Anger
nodes.full_label: Can an angry argument still be logical? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Tone Vs Logic
nodes.catchy_title: Can an angry argument still be logical?
nodes.summary: Emotional language is not a fallacy unless it replaces evidence, pressures the audience, or distracts from the claim being tested.

nodes.label: Credibility
nodes.full_label: When is a personal criticism relevant? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Tone Vs Logic
nodes.catchy_title: When is a personal criticism relevant?
nodes.summary: Personal criticism can be relevant when it bears directly on testimony, trust, or a role-specific duty rather than replacing the argument.

nodes.label: Four Tests
nodes.full_label: The four tests every argument faces | Logical Fallacies 998914 Tone Vs Logic
nodes.catchy_title: The four tests every argument faces
nodes.summary: A single statement can be logically strong, socially harmful, ethically poor, or strategically unpersuasive at the same time.

nodes.label: Polite Weakness
nodes.full_label: Why polite arguments can still be bad | Logical Fallacies 998914 Tone Vs Logic
nodes.catchy_title: Why polite arguments can still be bad
nodes.summary: Civil phrasing can disguise weak reasoning when status words, reassurance, or vague authority replace evidence for the conclusion.

nodes.label: Tone Policing
nodes.full_label: When does tone policing become a fallacy? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Tone Vs Logic
nodes.catchy_title: When does tone policing become a fallacy?
nodes.summary: Tone policing becomes a reasoning problem when criticism of delivery is used to avoid answering relevant claims or evidence.

nodes.label: Tradition
nodes.full_label: Is Old the Same as Right? | Logical Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: Is Old the Same as Right?
nodes.summary: Appeal to tradition treats age or familiarity as proof that a practice is correct or still justified.

nodes.label: Old Rules
nodes.full_label: When Should Old Rules Stay? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Appeal To Tradition
nodes.catchy_title: When Should Old Rules Stay?
nodes.summary: Old rules deserve investigation before removal, but their age alone cannot prove they still solve the right problem.

nodes.label: Semmelweis
nodes.full_label: When Medical Tradition Cost Lives | Logical Fallacies 998914 Appeal To Tradition
nodes.catchy_title: When Medical Tradition Cost Lives
nodes.summary: Semmelweis's handwashing case shows how professional habit can resist evidence even when lives are at stake.

nodes.label: Status Quo
nodes.full_label: Why Familiar Choices Feel Safer | Logical Fallacies 998914 Appeal To Tradition
nodes.catchy_title: Why Familiar Choices Feel Safer
nodes.summary: Familiar options can feel less risky even when nobody has compared them fairly with available alternatives.

nodes.label: Time Tested
nodes.full_label: What Has Time Really Tested? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Appeal To Tradition
nodes.catchy_title: What Has Time Really Tested?
nodes.summary: Calling a practice time-tested is useful only after asking what outcomes, conditions and alternatives were really tested.

nodes.label: Traditional Roles
nodes.full_label: Does Tradition Make Roles Fair? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Appeal To Tradition
nodes.catchy_title: Does Tradition Make Roles Fair?
nodes.summary: A role being traditional does not show that exclusion, hierarchy or unequal treatment is fair today.

nodes.label: Tu Quoque
nodes.full_label: Does Hypocrisy Refute the Claim? | Logical Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: Does Hypocrisy Refute the Claim?
nodes.summary: Tu quoque replies point to inconsistency in the speaker, but that does not automatically answer the claim.

nodes.label: Credibility
nodes.full_label: When Hypocrisy Really Hurts Credibility | Logical Fallacies 998914 Tu Quoque
nodes.catchy_title: When Hypocrisy Really Hurts Credibility
nodes.summary: Hypocrisy matters most when the claim depends on personal trust, authority, sincerity or special competence.

nodes.label: Double Standards
nodes.full_label: When Double Standards Are the Point | Logical Fallacies 998914 Tu Quoque
nodes.catchy_title: When Double Standards Are the Point
nodes.summary: Pointing out inconsistency can be directly relevant when the dispute is about fair enforcement or equal treatment.

nodes.label: Feasibility
nodes.full_label: Does Hypocrisy Reveal Hidden Costs? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Tu Quoque
nodes.catchy_title: Does Hypocrisy Reveal Hidden Costs?
nodes.summary: A speaker's failure to follow an easy-sounding rule may reveal that the proposal is harder than advertised.

nodes.label: Smoking Doctor
nodes.full_label: Can a Hypocrite Still Give Good Advice? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Tu Quoque
nodes.catchy_title: Can a Hypocrite Still Give Good Advice?
nodes.summary: A hypocritical doctor can still give sound health advice when the warning rests on evidence rather than personal example.

nodes.label: Whataboutism
nodes.full_label: When Whataboutism Dodges the Real Issue | Logical Fallacies 998914 Tu Quoque
nodes.catchy_title: When Whataboutism Dodges the Real Issue
nodes.summary: Whataboutism can expose double standards, but it often dodges the original accusation instead of answering it.

nodes.label: Wet Pavement
nodes.full_label: Why One Explanation Is Not Enough | Logical Fallacies
nodes.catchy_title: Why One Explanation Is Not Enough
nodes.summary: Affirming the consequent shows why one possible explanation is not the same as the only explanation.

nodes.label: Driver Example
nodes.full_label: Does No Accident Prove Good Driving? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Affirming Consequent
nodes.catchy_title: Does No Accident Prove Good Driving?
nodes.summary: Avoiding accidents may suggest good driving, but luck, low mileage, and easy roads can explain the same result.

nodes.label: One Way Logic
nodes.full_label: Why If P Then Q Does Not Reverse | Logical Fallacies 998914 Affirming Consequent
nodes.catchy_title: Why If P Then Q Does Not Reverse
nodes.summary: A conditional promise only runs one way unless the statement also says the outcome cannot happen any other way.

nodes.label: Other Causes
nodes.full_label: What Else Could Make Pavement Wet? | Logical Fallacies 998914 Affirming Consequent
nodes.catchy_title: What Else Could Make Pavement Wet?
nodes.summary: Wet pavement can point to rain, but street cleaning, sprinklers, leaks, or flooding can make the same observation misleading.

nodes.label: Smoke and Fire
nodes.full_label: When Bad Logic Still Feels Sensible | Logical Fallacies 998914 Affirming Consequent
nodes.catchy_title: When Bad Logic Still Feels Sensible
nodes.summary: Some effect-to-cause guesses are useful in real life, but they are not deductive proof unless other causes are ruled out.

nodes.label: Truth Table
nodes.full_label: The Truth Table That Breaks the Rain Claim | Logical Fallacies 998914 Affirming Consequent
nodes.catchy_title: The Truth Table That Breaks the Rain Claim
nodes.summary: A truth table shows the exact row where wet pavement and a true conditional still leave rain unproven.
